# Optimal Site Generator Distribution

**Data Sources:**

-   Proprietary Telecommunications Company data, localised to Cape Town and some surrounding areas.

-   City of Cape Town Loadshedding Area data

-   Eskom Se Push Historical Loadshedding Stages Cape Town

## Problem Statement

Load shedding and an insecure power supply place a strain on network sites, reducing their coverage and availability and materially affecting the revenue they generate from user traffic. Running generators at sites affected by power disruptions is an immediate way to keep them operating during interruptions. However, only a limited number of generators can be deployed, and deploying and running them is costly. The Telecommunications Company would like to develop a strategy for allocating generators optimally to important sites at minimum cost, while ensuring that coverage and availability requirements are maintained.

## Key Definitions

**Atoll Site ID:** A unique identifier for a network site in the Atoll radio planning tool [@forsk2015]. A site is a physical location that houses the antennas, transmitters, receivers and networking hardware used to transmit and receive voice, data and internet signals. Each site has a defined coverage area, represented as a polygon, which describes the extent of its service over the surrounding geography.

# Section 1: Deterministic MLP Formulation

The generator deployment problem lends itself to the set covering formulation. In this case, we would like to deploy generators the minimum number of sites subject to the additional constraint that at least 90% of total subscribers at full peak/availability can access the network during times of load shedding.

To necessitate this, a few key assumptions have to made:

-   Each site can get only one generator. All cells for each technology (2G,3G,4G,5G) are fully powered by said generator on the site.

-   Assume a Stage 1- type load shedding schedule with at most 1 power outage per day for 2.5hrs .Load shedding affects all sites at the same time. Load shedding happens at peak hours/demand across sites.

-   Subscriber location. All subscribers of site $i$ are treated as located at site $i$, so they are either entirely within reach of a powered site or not. This assumes concentrated subscriber densities.

-   Subscribers can connect coverage/network of neighboring sites fluidly (if they are within the average site perimeter). Thus is if one site goes one, and another site within the overlap radius has a generator, then the a subscriber within that radius can access the generator-ran site's network/coverage with no signal degradation at site edges.

-   Unlimited absorption. A powered site can absorb all subscribers of every site within its radius, with no capacity limit.

-   Peak demand. $w_i$ is the subscriber count at site $i$ at full peak. Coverage target. At least 90% of total peak subscribers must be served during the outage.

-   Each site has a coverage area, drawn as a polygon on the map. Two sites are considered neighbours if their coverage areas touch, and also assume a generator at one site can also cover its neighbours' subscribers. This is recorded in a table of ones and zeros, $a_{ij}$, which equals 1 when sites $i$ and $j$ are the same or neighbours, a standard device in coverage models [@churchrevelle1974]. Touching is measured as the shortest straight-line distance between the two areas, computed in metres with the `sf` package [@pebesma2018]. A small tolerance of 10 m counts areas that almost meet as touching, to allow for drawing errors. Unlike a fixed distance, this rule adapts to local site size, so a dense urban site does not reach unrealistically many neighbours.

### Formulation

$$
\begin{aligned}
I &: \text{set of sites, indexed by } i, j \\
P_i &: \text{coverage cell (polygon) of site } i \\
d(P_i, P_j) &: \text{minimum distance between the coverage cells of sites } i \text{ and } j \text{ (m)} \\
\varepsilon &= 10 \text{ m} : \text{tolerance for digitisation error, so that cells sharing a boundary are adjacent} \\
a_{ij} &=
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } i = j \ \text{ or } \ d(P_i, P_j) \le \varepsilon \quad (\text{so } a_{ii} = 1) \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
w_i &: \text{peak unique subscribers at site } i \\
\beta &= 0.90 : \text{minimum fraction of total subscribers that must be served}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Decision variables

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_j &\in \{0,1\} && \text{1 if a generator is deployed at site } j \\
y_i &\in \{0,1\} && \text{1 if the subscribers of site } i \text{ are served during the outage}
\end{aligned}
$$

### Model

Minimize the number of generators deployed:

$$
\min \sum_{j \in I} x_j
$$ {#eq-obj}

subject to

$$
y_i \le \sum_{j \in I} a_{ij}\, x_j \qquad \forall i \in I
$$ {#eq-cover}

$$
\sum_{i \in I} w_i\, y_i \ge \beta \sum_{i \in I} w_i
$$ {#eq-target}

$$
x_j \in \{0,1\}, \quad y_i \in \{0,1\} \qquad \forall i, j \in I
$$ {#eq-domain}

```{r,solve_LP, echo=F, eval=T}


n=nrow(neigh_mat)
# order of obj, xi,yi
obj_vec=c( rep(1,nrow(neigh_mat)),rep(0, nrow(neigh_mat)) ) # xi



constraint_mat_lp=rbind(constraint_1,constraint_2)

my_types = rep("B", 2 * nrow(neigh_mat)) #rep("B",length(obj_vec)) # enforces boolean output!
rhs_=c(rep(0, n), beta * total_subs)#rbind(rhs_1,rhs_2)
dir_vec=c(rep('<=',nrow(neigh_mat)),'>=')

# Enter into solver


lp_soln=Rglpk_solve_LP(obj = obj_vec, mat =constraint_mat_lp , types = my_types,dir = dir_vec, rhs = rhs_, max = FALSE) # minimization problm



```

```{r,check,eval=T,include=F}
# ---- 3. Exact LP (same model as before) -------------------------------------
solve_cover <- function(A, w, beta){
  n  <- nrow(A); ws <- w / sum(w)
  res <- Rglpk_solve_LP(
    obj   = c(rep(1, n), rep(0, n)),
    mat   = rbind(cbind(-A, diag(n)), c(rep(0, n), ws)),
    dir   = c(rep("<=", n), ">="),
    rhs   = c(rep(0, n), beta),
    types = rep("B", 2 * n), max = FALSE)
  x <- round(res$solution[1:n])                          # generators only
  out <- data.frame(mean_reach    = round(mean(colSums(A)), 1),
                    generators    = sum(x),
                    covered_share = round(sum(w[as.vector(A %*% x) >= 1]) / sum(w), 4),
                    status        = res$status)
  attr(out, "x") <- x                                    # chosen generator sites
  out
}

  "Radius 3 km"                  = A_rad(3000),
  "Own range x 2"                = A_own(2)
)
```

**Key Observation from LP formulation\
**The linear programme gives an exact answer what the fewest generators needed so that at least 90% of subscribers sit at a site that either hosts a generator or touches a site that does.\
Its core strength is that the optimum is provably the best possible for that (albeit simple) formulation, and the used the neighbourhood definition. However, it has some limitations

-   It does not cater for the importance of or ranking of the site in terms of its revenue metrics.

-   The model is static: it assumes every supported site can draw on its generator at the same time, and it ignores load-shedding schedules, generator capacity and the randomness of the stage

-   The single objective also hides a trade-off: it minimises the number of generators and is indifferent to which 10% of subscribers are left uncovered, so the multi-objective view shows whether those uncovered sites are disproportionately high-revenue sites.\

# Section 2: Deterministic MOLP Formulation- Incorporating Revenue-led Site Importance

Naturally, the choice to deploy a generator at a site is not only determined by cost alone, but by the relative importance of the site in terms of its traffic flows and revenue. Thus an additional objective to the problem would be to minimize (or at least preserve) aggregate peak traffic flow loss across sites and thus minimize (at least preserve) peak revenue loss at these sites.

For simplicity's sake (and available data), assume the following, in addition to the key assumptions in Section 1:

-   Revenue at a site,$Rev_i$, is a monotonically increasing function of traffic. Thus, a relatively high-revenue site implies that a high-traffic site.

-   As such, only the revenue objective is added to the initial generator minimization problem, with the aim to minimize the loss of revenue at these sites. The average monthly site revenues are generated at peak times across sites. The sum of these across sites would ideally be preserved or maximised.

-   **Revenue follows the subscriber:** The traffic/revenue that would be ordinarily attributed to a site before loadshedding, can be "absorbed" into neighboring sites by virtue of the subscribers still being able to access neigbouring sites that have generators as assumed in Section 1.

-   We initially assume that revenue preservation and generator cost minimization are weighted equally: $w1=w2=0.5$

### Additional parameters

Let $R_i$ denote the revenue of network site $i \in I$. Normalise each KPI to $[0,1]$:

$$\{r}_i = \frac{Rev_i - \min_k Rev_k}{\max_k Rev_k - \min_k Rev_k},
\qquad
$$

Variable Definitions:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_i &: \text{average monthly peak revenue at site } i \\
G &: \text{target (budget) number of generators} \\
\gamma=0.95 &: \text{target fraction of total peak revenue preserved} \\
\omega_1, \omega_2 &: \text{goal weights}, \; \omega_1 + \omega_2 = 1 \\
d_G^{+} &\ge 0 : \text{generators deployed above target } G \\
d_r^{-} &\ge 0 : \text{shortfall of preserved revenue below target } \gamma \textstyle\sum_i r_i
\end{aligned}
$$

#### Weighted Archimedian Formulation

$$
\min \;\; \omega_1 \frac{d_G^{+}}{G} \;+\; \omega_2 \frac{d_r^{-}}{\gamma \sum_{i \in I} r_i}
$$ {#eq-gp-obj}

subject to the original constraints

$$
y_i \le \sum_{j \in I} a_{ij}\, x_j \qquad \forall i \in I
$$ {#eq-gp-cover}

$$
\sum_{i \in I} w_i\, y_i \ge \beta \sum_{i \in I} w_i
$$ {#eq-gp-target}

and the two goal constraints

$$
\sum_{j \in I} x_j - d_G^{+} \le G
$$ {#eq-gp-goal-gen}

$$
\sum_{i \in I} r_i\, y_i + d_r^{-} \ge \gamma \sum_{i \in I} r_i
$$ {#eq-gp-goal-rev}

$$
x_j \in \{0,1\}, \quad y_i \in [0,1], \quad d_G^{+}, d_r^{-} \ge 0
$$ {#eq-gp-domain}

Where $G$ is the **initial optimal solution** from the **LP formulation in Section 1.**

```{r,goal_set_up, eval=T, echo=FALSE,include=F}

# we want to preserve the normalized revenue
```

```{r,mogp_arch_soln, eval=T,echo=F ,include=F}


# order of obj (dg,dr,x1,x2,....,xn, y1,y2,....yn) yi is the revenue that is still preserved at a site if it either got a generator OR that ,xi s ite
obj_vec_ac=c(dg_coeff,dr_coeff,xn_coeff,yn_coeff)

constraint_mat_arc=rbind(g1_constraints,g2_constraint,a1,a2); dim(constraint_mat_arc)

my_types_b = rep("B",(  length(xn_coeff)+(length(yn_coeff) ))) # enforces boolean output for xi, yi!
my_types_c = rep("C",1) # continuous output for dr
my_types_i = rep("I",1) # integer output for dg

my_types_ar=c(my_types_i,my_types_c,my_types_b );length(my_types_ar)


rhs_=rbind(matrix(G1,nrow=1,ncol=1),  matrix(G2,nrow=1,ncol=1),rhs_1,rhs_2)
dir_vec=c('<=','>=',rep('<=',dim(constraint_1)[1]),'>=');length(dir_vec)

# Enter into solver


mogp_arc_soln=Rglpk_solve_LP(obj = obj_vec_ac, mat =constraint_mat_arc , types = my_types_ar,dir = dir_vec, rhs = rhs_, max = FALSE) # minimization problm

 mogp_arc_soln # Interprete tomorrow
```

```{r,mogp_arc_soln_summ,echo=F}
# ---- 1. Inputs aligned to A_adj ------------------------------------------------

site_rev_ranking=st_drop_geometry(cpt_site_ranges_rev_gdf) %>% arrange(desc(monthly_rev)) %>% mutate(rev_ranking=row_number()) %>% select(atoll_site_id,rev_ranking)

stopifnot(!anyNA(w))

# ---- 2. Decode the two solutions ------------------------------------------------

# ---- 3. Score a placement the same way for both solutions ----------------------
score <- function(x){
  covered <- as.vector(A %*% x) >= 1
  chosen  <- which(x == 1)
  c(generators       = sum(x),
    subs_covered     = sum(w[covered]) / sum(w),
    revenue_covered  = sum(r[covered], na.rm = TRUE) / sum(r, na.rm = TRUE),
    sites_supported  = mean(covered),
    median_rank      = median(rk[chosen], na.rm = TRUE),
    best_rank        = min(rk[chosen], na.rm = TRUE),
    top25_count      = sum(rk[chosen] <= 0.25 * N_ranked, na.rm = TRUE))
}

s_base <- score(x_base)
s_goal <- score(x_goal)

fmt_pct <- function(p) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * p)

  `Goal programme`      = c(s_goal["generators"],

                            s_goal["median_rank"],

                            s_goal["top25_count"]),
  check.names = FALSE
)

kable(compare_tbl, align = c("l", "r", "r"),
      caption = "Single-objective LP versus weighted goal programme")

# ---- 5. Table 2: goal deviations and trade-off --------------------------------------
extra_gens <- sum(x_goal) - sum(x_base)
rev_gain_pp <- 100 * (s_goal["revenue_covered"] - s_base["revenue_covered"])

            both, added, dropped,
            sprintf("%.4f", mogp_arc_soln$optimum))
)

kable(dev_tbl, align = c("l", "r"),

chosen_tbl <- tibble(atoll_site_id = ids,
```

**Sensitivity Analysis**

Vary the goal weights to see how the model solution and accompanying metrics change.

```{r}
# =============================================================================
# Sensitivity of the weighted Archimedean goal programme to its weights
#
# Objective:  w1 * d_G+ / G1  +  w2 * d_r- / G2        with  w2 = 1 - w1
# Only the two deviation coefficients change between runs; the constraint
# matrix, directions, right-hand side and variable types are reused as is.
#
# Variable order in the solver:  (d_G+, d_r-, x_1..x_n, y_1..y_n)
#
# Assumes in the session (all from your existing setup):
#   constraint_mat_arc, dir_vec, rhs_, my_types_ar, G1, G2
#   A_adj, cpt_site_ranges_subs_gdf, rev_df, site_rev_ranking
#
# NOT RUN by the author - adapt names where needed.
# In Quarto, put each plot / kable() call as the last line of its own chunk.
# =============================================================================
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(Rglpk)
library(knitr)
library(sf)

# ---- 0. Inputs aligned to A_adj (skip any that you already have) -------------
n       <- nrow(A_adj)
A       <- matrix(as.numeric(A_adj), nrow = n, ncol = n)
site_df <- st_drop_geometry(cpt_site_ranges_subs_gdf)
ids     <- site_df$atoll_site_id
w       <- as.numeric(site_df$avg_nr_unique_subs)
r       <- rev_df$monthly_rev[match(ids, rev_df$atoll_site_id)]
rk      <- site_rev_ranking$rev_ranking[match(ids, site_rev_ranking$atoll_site_id)]
N_ranked <- nrow(site_rev_ranking)

# ---- 1. Settings ----------------------------------------------------------------
# Tiny cost on each x so that, among solutions that tie on the two goals, the one
# with the FEWEST generators is returned. Set to 0 to reproduce your model exactly.
eps_x <- 1e-5

# Weight grid. The ends (w1 = 0 or 1) are left out on purpose: with one weight at
# zero the other goal is ignored and the solution is arbitrary.
w1_grid <- c(0.25,0.5,0.75)#sort(unique(c(seq(0, 0.95, by = 0.25), 0.5)))

# ---- 2. Solve once for a given w1 ----------------------------------------------------
run_mogp <- function(w1){
  w2  <- 1 - w1
  obj <- c(w1 / G1, w2 / G2, rep(eps_x, n), rep(0, n))

  res <- Rglpk_solve_LP(obj = obj, mat = constraint_mat_arc, dir = dir_vec,
                        rhs = as.numeric(rhs_), types = my_types_ar, max = FALSE)

  if (res$status != 0) {
    warning(sprintf("w1 = %.2f: solver status %s", w1, res$status))
    return(list(row = data.frame(w1 = w1, w2 = w2, status = res$status),
                x = rep(NA_real_, n)))
  }

  sol     <- res$solution
  x       <- round(sol[3:(n + 2)])                    # generators only
  covered <- as.vector(A %*% x) >= 1
  chosen  <- which(x == 1)

  list(
    row = data.frame(
      w1 = w1, w2 = w2, status = res$status,
      generators      = sum(x),
      d_G_plus        = sol[1],
      d_r_minus       = sol[2],
      subs_covered    = sum(w[covered]) / sum(w),
      revenue_covered = sum(r[covered], na.rm = TRUE) / sum(r, na.rm = TRUE),
      sites_supported = mean(covered),
      median_rank     = median(rk[chosen], na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_rank       = mean(rk[chosen], na.rm = TRUE),
      top25_count     = sum(rk[chosen] <= 0.25 * N_ranked, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    x = x
  )
}

# ---- 3. Sweep ------------------------------------------------------------------------
runs    <- lapply(w1_grid, run_mogp)
results <- bind_rows(lapply(runs, `[[`, "row"))
X_mat   <- do.call(rbind, lapply(runs, `[[`, "x"))      # rows = weights, columns = sites

ok <- results$status == 0

# ---- 4. Results table ------------------------------------------------------------------
results_tbl <- results %>%
  filter(status == 0) %>%
  transmute(`w1`                  = sprintf("%.2f", w1),
            `w2`                  = sprintf("%.2f", w2),
            `Generators`          = generators,
            `Extra over G`        = round(d_G_plus),
            `Subscribers covered` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * subs_covered),
            `Revenue covered`     = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * revenue_covered),
            `Sites supported`     = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * sites_supported),
            `Median revenue rank` = median_rank,
            `Sites in top 25%`    = top25_count)

kable(results_tbl, align = "r",
      caption = "Goal programme results across weight settings")

# ---- 5. Plot 1: each metric against the weights -------------------------------------------
metric_levels <- c("Generators deployed", "Revenue covered (%)",
                   "Subscribers covered (%)", "Sites supported (%)",
                   "Median revenue rank of generator sites",
                   "Generator sites in top 25% by revenue")

long <- results %>%
  filter(status == 0) %>%
  transmute(w1,
            `Generators deployed`                      = generators,
            `Revenue covered (%)`                      = 100 * revenue_covered,
            `Subscribers covered (%)`                  = 100 * subs_covered,
            `Sites supported (%)`                      = 100 * sites_supported,
            `Median revenue rank of generator sites`   = median_rank,
            `Generator sites in top 25% by revenue`    = top25_count) %>%
  pivot_longer(-w1, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = metric_levels))

ggplot(long, aes(x = w1, y = value)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(sec.axis = sec_axis(~ 1 - ., name = "w2 (weight on revenue goal)")) +
  labs(x = "w1 (weight on generator goal)", y = NULL,
       title = "How each outcome changes with the goal weights",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: original equal weights (0.5, 0.5)") +
  theme_minimal()

# ---- 6. Plot 2: the trade-off frontier ---------------------------------------------------------
ggplot(filter(results, status == 0),
       aes(x = generators, y = 100 * revenue_covered, colour = w1)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey75") +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", w1)), vjust = -0.9, size = 3, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "w1") +
  labs(x = "Generators deployed", y = "Revenue covered (%)",
       title = "Trade-off between generators and revenue covered",
       subtitle = "Labels show w1; w2 = 1 - w1") +
  theme_minimal()

# ---- 7. Plot 3: which sites are chosen at each weight -------------------------------------------
ever <- which(colSums(X_mat == 1, na.rm = TRUE) > 0)       # sites chosen at least once
cat("Sites chosen in at least one run:", length(ever), "\n")
cat("Sites chosen in EVERY run       :",
    sum(colSums(X_mat == 1, na.rm = TRUE) == sum(ok)), "\n")

tile_df <- data.frame(
  w1     = rep(w1_grid, times = length(ever)),
  site   = rep(ids[ever], each = length(w1_grid)),
  rank   = rep(rk[ever],  each = length(w1_grid)),
  chosen = as.vector(X_mat[, ever])
) %>%
  filter(!is.na(chosen)) %>%
  mutate(site = factor(site, levels = ids[ever][order(rk[ever])]),
         w1   = factor(sprintf("%.2f", w1)))

ggplot(tile_df, aes(x = w1, y = site, fill = factor(chosen))) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
```

# Section 3: Simulated Annealing Formulation\*

To apply simulated annealing on the initial LP formulation, the constrained optimization problem is transformed to its Langrangian representation which essentially incorporates the constraints of the LP problem into the objective function that will be minimized.

## Lagrangian formulations of the set covering problem

### Assumptions

\begin{enumerate}
\item The candidate generator locations coincide with the demand sites $I$,
and $a_{ii} = 1$ (a generator covers its own site).
\item Coverage is binary and deterministic: $a_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$.
\item Weights $w_i \ge 0$ are fixed, and $0 < \beta \le 1$ is the required covered fraction of $W = \sum_{i \in I} w_i$.
\item For fixed $\mathbf{x}$ the best choice is $y_i = \min\{1, \sum_{j} a_{ij} x_j\}$,
so $y$ can be eliminated: $C(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i \in I} w_i\, \mathbb{1}\{\sum_{j} a_{ij} x_j \ge 1\}$.
\end{enumerate}

### Original problem

$$
z^{*} = \min \sum_{j \in I} x_j
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad
y_i \le \sum_{j \in I} a_{ij} x_j \;\; \forall i, \quad
\sum_{i \in I} w_i y_i \ge \beta W, \quad
x_j, y_i \in \{0,1\}.
$$

### Formulation 1: relax the coverage target (multiplier $\lambda \ge 0$)

$$
g_1(\lambda) = \lambda \beta W + \min_{\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^{I}}
\Big\{ \sum_{j \in I} x_j - \lambda\, C(\mathbf{x}) \Big\}
\;\le\; z^{*}.
$$

The inner problem is a prize-collecting covering problem and is solved by simulated annealing.

### Formulation 2: relax the linking constraints (multipliers $\mu_i \ge 0$)

$$
g_2(\boldsymbol{\mu}) = \sum_{j \in I} \min\Big\{0,\; 1 - \sum_{i \in I} a_{ij} \mu_i\Big\}
+ \min_{\mathbf{y} \in \{0,1\}^{I}} \Big\{ \sum_{i \in I} \mu_i y_i \;:\; \sum_{i \in I} w_i y_i \ge \beta W \Big\}
\;\le\; z^{*}.
$$\

The problem separates into independent decisions on $x_j$ and a knapsack-cover problem in $y$. Maximise $g_2$ over $\boldsymbol{\mu} \ge 0$ by subgradient steps, giving a lower bound.

### Penalised objective used by simulated annealing

$$
F_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j \in I} x_j + \lambda \max\{0,\; \beta W - C(\mathbf{x})\}.
$$

If $w_i$ are positive integers and the target is $\lceil \beta W \rceil$, any $\lambda > 1$ makes every minimiser of $F_{\lambda}$ feasible.

```{r}
# Solving the above

# =============================================================================
# Simulated annealing for generator placement (penalised Lagrangian objective)
#
#   F(x) = sum_j x_j + lambda * max(0, beta*W - C(x))
#
#   x_j  = 1 if a generator is placed at site j
#   C(x) = total weight of sites covered by at least one placed generator
#   W    = total weight, beta = required covered fraction
#
# Same building blocks as the SA examples: initial solution, evaluate, perturb,
# geometric cooling, accept/reject.
# =============================================================================

set.seed(100)   # for repeatability

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data  (REPLACE THIS BLOCK WITH YOUR OWN)
#    A : n x n 0/1 coverage matrix, A[i, j] = 1 if site i is in the coverage
#        polygon of a generator at j (set the diagonal to 1)

# site_imp=st_drop_geometry(cpt_site_ranges_rev_gdf)
# site_imp$site_imp_weigt=site_imp$rev_norm/sum(site_imp$rev_norm)
#site_imp %>% arrange(desc(site_imp_weigt))

# A=neigh_mat
# dim(A)
# w= sub_coeff # vectore of site importances
# n   <- dim(neigh_mat)[1]
# 
# beta   <- 0.9              # required covered fraction for subscribers
# W      <- sum(w)
# target <- beta * W             # (use ceiling(beta * W) if weights are integers)
# 
# # Penalty weight. lambda > 1 / min(w) makes every minimiser of F feasible,
# # because covering one uncovered site then always pays for the generator.
# lambda <- 2 / min(w[w > 0])


A    = A_adj#neigh_mat          # same matrix the LP used
diag(A) = 1
w    = sub_coeff          # same weights the LP used
beta = 0.9                # same target the LP used (the SA run earlier used 0.95)
n    = nrow(A)
stopifnot(length(w) == n, all(A %in% c(0, 1)))

W      <- sum(w)
target <- beta * W
lambda <- 2 / min(w[w > 0])

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Evaluation function
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
covered_weight <- function(x){
  covered <- as.vector(A %*% x) >= 1
  sum(w[covered])
}

covered_weight(rbinom(n, 1, 0.8))

evaluate_x <- function(x){
  shortfall <- max(0, target - covered_weight(x))
  sum(x) + lambda * shortfall
}

is_feasible <- function(x){
  covered_weight(x) >= target - 1e-9
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Initial solution
#    Random placement. A good starting point helps: you could instead start
#    from a greedy solution or from all sites (always feasible).
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
get_initial_x <- function(n){
  rbinom(n, 1, 0.8)
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Perturbation: flip one site, or swap a placed and an unplaced generator
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# x is our candidate soln at current iteration
perturb_x <- function(x){
  ones  <- which(x == 1)
  zeros <- which(x == 0)

  if(runif(1) < 0.5 || length(ones) == 0 || length(zeros) == 0){
    # flip a random site
    j <- sample.int(length(x), 1)
    x[j] <- 1 - x[j]
  } else {
    # swap: move one generator to a currently unplaced site
    j <- ones[sample.int(length(ones), 1)]
    k <- zeros[sample.int(length(zeros), 1)]
    x[j] <- 0
    x[k] <- 1
  }
  return(x)
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Repair: drop redundant generators while the target stays met
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
repair_x <- function(x){
  repeat{
    ones <- which(x == 1)
    if(length(ones) == 0) break
    cov_without <- sapply(ones, function(j){
      y <- x
      y[j] <- 0
      covered_weight(y)
    })
    ok <- cov_without >= target - 1e-9
    if(!any(ok)) break
    j <- ones[ok][which.max(cov_without[ok])]   # remove the least useful one
    x[j] <- 0
  }
  return(x)
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Simulated annealing
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
start_temp  <- 5
temp_factor <- 0.9995
n_iter      <- 50000

cur_x  <- get_initial_x(n);sum(get_initial_x(n))
cur_fx <- evaluate_x(cur_x)

# results (pre-allocated, as storing every solution gets slow for large n)
all_fx   <- numeric(n_iter)
all_ngen <- numeric(n_iter)
all_feas <- logical(n_iter)

best_x <- NULL            # best FEASIBLE solution seen (fewest generators)

for(i in 1:n_iter){

  # generate a candidate solution
  prop_x <- perturb_x(cur_x)

  # evaluate the candidate solution
  prop_fx <- evaluate_x(prop_x)

  # calculate the probability of accepting the candidate
  anneal_temp <- start_temp * temp_factor ^ i
  accept_prob <- exp(-(prop_fx - cur_fx) / anneal_temp)

  # accept or reject the candidate
  if(prop_fx < cur_fx){
    cur_x  <- prop_x
    cur_fx <- prop_fx
  } else {
    if(runif(1) < accept_prob){
      cur_x  <- prop_x
      cur_fx <- prop_fx
    }
  }

  # keep the best feasible solution (fewest generators)
  if(is_feasible(cur_x) && (is.null(best_x) || sum(cur_x) < sum(best_x))){
    best_x <- cur_x
  }

  # store results
  all_fx[i]   <- cur_fx
  all_ngen[i] <- sum(cur_x)
  all_feas[i] <- is_feasible(cur_x)
}

if(is.null(best_x)){
  stop("No feasible solution found: increase n_iter, start_temp or lambda.")
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Results
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
#best_x <- repair_x(best_x)

cat("Generators placed       :", sum(best_x), "\n")
cat("Covered weight fraction :", round(covered_weight(best_x) / W, 4),
    "(target", beta, ")\n")
cat("Selected sites          :", which(best_x == 1), "\n")

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(all_fx, type = "l", xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "Penalised objective F(x)")
plot(all_ngen, type = "l", xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "Generators in current solution")
plot(1:n_iter, start_temp * temp_factor ^ (1:n_iter), type = "l",
     xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "Temperature")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

```

### Properties

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Weak duality:} $g_1(\lambda) \le z^{*}$ and $g_2(\boldsymbol{\mu}) \le z^{*}$ for all multipliers $\ge 0$.
\item \textbf{Duality gap:} the problem is integer, so $\max_{\lambda} g_1$ and $\max_{\boldsymbol{\mu}} g_2$ can be strictly below $z^{*}$.
\item \textbf{Role of SA:} it supplies a feasible upper bound $\sum_j x_j^{\text{best}}$, and the
Lagrangian supplies the lower bound, giving a reportable gap.
\end{itemize}

# Section 4:Discrete Event Simulation for Stochastic Load Shedding Scheduling

What is different:\
One of my key assumptions initial LP formulation is that the load shedding schedule is deterministic and that all sites are experience power outages at the same time. In reality this is not the case.

There is a stochastic element to the prevalence of the power outages and as such not all sites will experiance interrupted power at the same time and require generators. In light of this, the problem is formulated as a discrete event and run simulations based on the appropriate statistical distributions of the loadshedding event.

Key Assumptions:

-   The loadshedding stage for a given day is stochastic and as such follows an appropriate statistical distribution, however, the actual load shedding times that come as a result of that announced stage are deterministic and follow a set schedule.

-   Only a percetange of sites are affected by load shedding at the same time. The percentage at any given schedule is deterministic.

### Empirical distribution of the weekly stage

Let $s_w \in \{0,1,\dots,8\}$ be the load-shedding stage in week $w$, defined as the most occurring stage over that week in the historical record ($N$ weeks in total, of which $n_k$ were at stage $k$). The stage is sampled from the empirical probability mass function $$
\hat{\pi}_k = \Pr(s_w = k) = \frac{n_k}{N}, \qquad k = 0,1,\dots,8,
\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{8} \hat{\pi}_k = 1,
$$ with no parametric distribution assumed. Sampling uses inverse transform: draw $U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ and set $$
\sigma_w = \min\Big\{k : \hat{F}(k) \ge U\Big\}, \qquad
\hat{F}(k) = \sum_{m=0}^{k} \hat{\pi}_m .
$$

```{r}
  group_by(week_date) %>%
```
